header.contentArea: Paediatric surgery: neonatal and infant intestinal obstruction

brief.scenario: A 4-week-old infant, Rory Penhallow, born at term, has abdominal distension, poor feeding and delayed passage of meconium: he first passed meconium at 72 hours of age. His parents report vomiting that has become green today.
brief.task: Assess this infant with suspected intestinal obstruction, explain urgent management and how Hirschsprung's disease is confirmed. You have 9 minutes. The examiner will give findings as you ask.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Distension, vomiting and delayed meconium mean obstruction until assessed by the paediatric surgeons.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Treating it as simple constipation with repeated laxatives.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: Call the paediatric and paediatric-surgical teams now; bilious vomiting is an emergency.

grid.label: Recognises red flags
grid.fail: Treats it as simple constipation and reassures the parents.
grid.pass: Recognises delayed meconium (more than 48 hours in a term infant), distension and vomiting as red flags for Hirschsprung's disease.
grid.high: States that normal meconium passage would not exclude the disease.

grid.label: Bilious vomiting
grid.pass: Bilious vomiting also requires urgent exclusion of malrotation/volvulus.
grid.high: Treats green vomiting as a surgical emergency and arranges assessment without delay.

grid.label: Urgent management
grid.pass: Arranges immediate paediatric and paediatric-surgical assessment; nil by mouth, IV access, glucose and electrolytes, hydration, resuscitation and gastric decompression.
grid.high: Coordinates resuscitation and decompression with the paediatric team in parallel with the surgical referral.

grid.label: Enterocolitis
grid.fail: Misses fever, lethargy or diarrhoea as signs of enterocolitis.
grid.pass: Recognises fever, lethargy, worsening distension, diarrhoea or shock as possible Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis needing emergency resuscitation and antimicrobials.
grid.high: Knows that decompression and rectal washouts require specialist direction.

grid.label: Confirming the diagnosis
grid.fail: Relies on anorectal manometry or explosive stool after rectal examination.
grid.pass: Rectal biopsy, usually suction biopsy in an infant, confirms aganglionosis when an adequate specimen is assessed by specialist pathology.
grid.high: States that anorectal manometry should not be used to exclude Hirschsprung's disease.

grid.label: Avoiding harm and explaining to parents
grid.fail: Repeats rectal examinations or sends the family home.
grid.pass: Avoids repeated rectal examinations and explains the urgency and next steps to the parents.
grid.high: Explains that definitive surgery is specialist and that nutrition and fluid status matter meanwhile.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Constipation is common in babies. I would reassure the parents.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Babies often posset. I would not worry about the colour.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Lactulose, and I would see him again in a week.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: He now has a fever and diarrhoea.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: That shows the laxative is working.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Anorectal manometry: if it is normal, it is not Hirschsprung's.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I am concerned about Hirschsprung's disease causing distal functional obstruction. Meconium after more than 48 hours in a term baby is a red flag, with distension and vomiting.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Bilious vomiting also requires urgent exclusion of malrotation/volvulus.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Arrange immediate paediatric and paediatric-surgical assessment for distension with vomiting. If obstruction is suspected, keep nil by mouth, obtain IV access, assess glucose/electrolytes and hydration, resuscitate as needed and arrange gastric decompression with the paediatric team.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: He now has a fever and diarrhoea.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Fever, lethargy, worsening distension, diarrhoea or shock may indicate Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis: initiate emergency resuscitation and senior-led antimicrobial treatment.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Rectal biopsy, usually suction biopsy in an infant, confirms aganglionosis when an adequate specimen is assessed by specialist pathology.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I would not repeat rectal examinations, and I would explain to his parents why he needs urgent assessment.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Hirschsprung's disease is likely, but normal meconium passage would not have excluded it, so I would not be reassured by that alone.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Green vomiting is a surgical emergency until assessed: malrotation with volvulus must be excluded urgently.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I would call the paediatric and paediatric-surgical teams now and, with the paediatric team, start resuscitation and gastric decompression while he is kept nil by mouth with IV access and glucose checked.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: He now has a fever and diarrhoea.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: This may be enterocolitis: emergency resuscitation and senior-led antimicrobials. Decompression/rectal washouts require specialist direction.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Suction rectal biopsy showing aganglionosis. Anorectal manometry should not be used to exclude Hirschsprung's disease.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I would explain to his parents that surgery is specialist and that his nutrition and fluids will be supported meanwhile.

failures.move: Ignores bilious vomiting in an infant.
failures.consequence: Malrotation with volvulus is missed. This is a critical fail.

failures.move: Uses anorectal manometry to exclude Hirschsprung's disease.

knowledge.fact: Meconium passed after more than 48 hours in a term baby is a red flag in a child with constipation.
Do not use anorectal manometry to exclude Hirschsprung's disease.
Bilious vomiting in a newborn or infant needs urgent surgical assessment to exclude malrotation with volvulus.

recall.say: “Green vomiting and delayed meconium: I need the paediatric surgeons now.”
do: Nil by mouth, IV access, glucose and electrolytes
Gastric decompression with the paediatric team

numbers.meaning: meconium later than this in a term baby is a red flag

partner.opening: This 4-week-old infant has abdominal distension, poor feeding, delayed meconium and vomiting. Assess him, explain urgent management and how Hirschsprung's disease is confirmed.
partner.actorBrief: If asked, the parents say the vomit has been green since this morning and he has had fewer wet nappies.

reveals.finding: He first passed meconium at 72 hours of age; he was born at term.
It has been green since this morning.

push.question: What else must you exclude with green vomiting?

curveballs.prompt: He now has a fever, diarrhoea and is more lethargic.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Possible enterocolitis: emergency resuscitation and senior-led antimicrobials; washouts under specialist direction.

curveballs.prompt: Is anorectal manometry enough to exclude it?
curveballs.safeAnswer: No: do not use anorectal manometry to exclude Hirschsprung's disease.
